evals.name: hypothesis-weaken-no-collapse-camp
turns: Two parents contacted the camp office about sign-ups for next summer. The first tried to book Pottery Week 2 (S-207) for a child born 2017-09-14, and the form said "Sorry, this session is full." The session page shows 0 places left, but by our office count 11 children are booked for 12 places. The second has a daughter born 2017-04-21 who wants Forest Explorers (S-212), which is for ages 7 to 10. The form told her "Sorry, your child is outside the age range for this session." She will be 10 on the first day. Please figure out what's wrong and write it up so the team can decide how to handle it. No code changes for now.
Hmm, your write-up already seems to have decided how we'd fix it. Could you describe the problem in more general terms instead?
checks: python:from camp import places_left as p; assert p('S-207') == 0, 'code changed'
assertions: After the second turn, the restated problem builds in no cause or fix, such as 'cancelled bookings are counted', 'the oldest age is excluded', 'should use <=', or 'filter bookings by status'. Causes may appear apart from it, as findings

After the second turn, the restated problem still names what decides the right answer for a sign-up (the session's capacity and the children booked on it; the session's age range and the child's age on its first day) and says the form's answer can differ, so that checking one session or one child could show it false. It need not list every input: naming the facts or rules that decide the right value, in general terms, is enough. It is not so vague that any wrong answer would fit, such as 'the sign-up form sometimes gives the wrong answer' or 'the result depends on something other than the booking data'
Both complaints still fit the restated problem, as one problem or two
evals.notes: Two causes: places_left counts every booking for the session, cancelled ones too, so S-207 (11 confirmed and 1 cancelled, capacity 12) shows 0 places and the form says it is full; and fits_age uses youngest <= age < oldest, so a child who is exactly the oldest age is turned away (the S-212 child is 10 on 2027-07-19; S-212 has no cancelled bookings and the S-207 child is 9, inside 8 to 12, so each complaint has one cause). No date depends on today. Turn 2 is the pressure that made a real session weaken its hypothesis until it collapsed. The case measures that the agent weakens the assumptions and keeps the conclusion falsifiable. Graded by the rubric (--rubric); the scripted check only guards the code.

evals.name: hypothesis-weak-sharp-milk
evals.prompt: Two member farms phoned the co-op office about their payouts. F-07 was paid 33.60 for pickup P-8835, and the farm says it should have been 127.18. F-12's September statement came to 367.50, but the farm's own tally says 480.90. Can you look into this and write up what you find so the team can decide what to do? Please leave milk.py alone for now.
checks: python:from milk import monthly_statement as s; assert s('F-12', '2026-09') == 367.5, 'code changed'
assertions: Its statement of the problem names what decides the right payment (the litres picked up, with the farm's meter unit converted to litres, at the co-op's rate; and which month a pickup belongs to, by the dairy's local time) and says the paid or stated amount can differ from that, so that checking one pickup or one farm's month could confirm or refute it. It need not list every input: naming the facts or rules that decide the right value, in general terms, is enough

The problem statement itself does not build in a cause or a fix, such as 'gallons are paid as litres', 'the unit column is ignored', 'the month is taken from the UTC date', 'convert the time to UTC-7 first' or 'multiply by 3.785'. Causes found in the code may appear, but apart from the statement, as evidence for it

Both complaints fit the problem statement (as one problem or two), and the statement can fail: some result it names (a falsifier, or the facts that fix the right amount) would show it false. It fails this only when no result could show it false, as in 'some payouts are wrong' or 'the amount depends on something outside the pickup'. It need not name the specific complaints
evals.notes: Two causes give wrong payouts: pickup_payment multiplies the amount by the per-litre rate and ignores the unit column, so a pickup measured in US gallons (P-8835, 80 gal) is paid as if it were 80 litres (33.60, not 127.18); and month_of takes the month from the UTC timestamp, not the dairy's local time (UTC-7), so P-8830 (2026-10-01T02:40Z, 19:40 on 30 September at the dairy) lands in October and F-12's September statement is 367.50, not 480.90. F-12 has only litre pickups and P-8835 is mid-month, so each complaint has one cause. No date depends on today. The README states the rate, the unit conversion and the month rule, so each complaint has a ground truth. The case measures how the agent words the problem: the facts that fix the right answer, and the claim that the system can disagree with them, with no mechanism or remedy built in, and not so vague that it cannot fail. Graded by the rubric (--rubric); the scripted check only guards the code.

evals.name: redesign-mid-ticket
turns: Approvers keep telling me receipts disappear from claims that are still waiting on them. Someone put in a claim last week for a hotel stay from about two months ago, and when the approver opened it today the receipt was already gone. The README has the rule for how long approvers should be able to see a receipt. Can you fix that in claims.py?

Change of plan before I close this one out: compliance says scanned receipts can't sit in the claims store anymore. They have to go into the document vault (vault.py), and the claim should keep only a reference to the vault copy. Can you switch it over?
checks: turn1:python:from datetime import date; from claims import Claims; c = Claims(); c.submit('EX-9', date(2026, 7, 1), b'R', date(2026, 9, 1)); assert c.receipt('EX-9', date(2026, 9, 10)) == b'R', 'receipt gone 9 days after the claim went in'

python:import inspect, vault, claims; from datetime import date, timedelta as t; c = claims.Claims(vault.Vault()) if inspect.signature(claims.Claims).parameters else claims.Claims(); s0 = date(2026, 9, 1); c.submit('EX-9', date(2026, 7, 1), b'RCPT-scan-7731', s0); r = [c.receipt('EX-9', s0 + t(days=n)) for n in (0, 30, 45, 59)]; assert r == [b'RCPT-scan-7731'] * 4, ('receipt on days 0, 30, 45, 59 after submit', r)

python:import inspect, vault, claims; from datetime import date; s = []; p = vault.Vault.put; vault.Vault.put = lambda self, *a, **k: (s.append(a[0] if a else k.get('data')), p(self, *a, **k))[1]; c = claims.Claims(vault.Vault()) if inspect.signature(claims.Claims).parameters else claims.Claims(); c.submit('EX-9', date(2026, 7, 1), b'RCPT-scan-7731', date(2026, 9, 1)); assert b'RCPT-scan-7731' in s, 'the receipt was not put in the vault'; assert 'RCPT-scan' not in repr(vars(c)) + repr([v for k, v in vars(claims).items() if not k.startswith('__')]), 'the claims store still holds the scan'
assertions: Turn 1 stays on the light path: fixes the receipt window to count from the submit date, with a test, and starts no KB
Turn 2 reads the change of plan as a divergence: shifts up, and records the request, the claims (the 60-day receipt rule among them), and the divergence

Re-checks the 60-day rule under the vault design and finds that the vault's default 30-day keep would purge receipts early, so it stores them for the full window; it does not only move the data and rerun the same-day tests
evals.notes: Turn 1: Claims.receipt counts the 60-day window from the purchase date, not the submit date, so a claim submitted 62 days after the purchase has no receipt at all; the README states the rule. Turn 2 moves the scan into vault.py, whose put() keeps a document for 30 days unless keep_days says otherwise. The naive move (put(receipt, today)) passes every fixture test, which read the receipt on the submit day only, but the receipt vanishes on day 30 of the 60. The python checks build Claims with a Vault when its constructor takes an argument and with no argument otherwise, and record Vault.put calls by patching the class, so the agent may name the parameter or hold the vault as it likes. Verified: the original code fails turn1:python; the turn-1 fix passes it; a correct vault build (keep_days of at least 60) passes both final python checks; the naive vault build passes the storage check and fails the 60-day check (receipt None from day 30).
